title: 5 Essential Items to Pack When Taking a Car to the Track

body_markdown:
Few things are more fun to a driver than getting a feel for what a car is capable of. The problem is that even mundane vehicles now pack the horsepower and torque to embarrass any speed limit, and advanced handling limits allow all but the squirrliest drivers to ignore the recommended speeds posted under curvy road signs. If you want to find out your and your car’s capabilities, it’s time to take it to the track, or at least a closed course.


Whether you choose a track day on a dedicated circuit or autocross in a parking lot or rallycross in a field, driving on a closed course puts your car outside normal operating conditions, and it’s smart to be prepared for unexpected problems. I wanted to do some testing and first hard pulls on my LS-swapped 1985 Corvette, and the street was just not the place to get a feel for it. I decided to head for the track. If you are thinking about doing the same, this list serves as a starting point for what to bring with you—just in case.


## Tools


Inside my van, I carry the most common items in a mechanic’s toolset.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Tire pressure gauge, jack, tire inflator, and torque wrench are all nice to have handy.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


There are two schools of thought on this one: Pack everything you could ever want or pack only the things you are prepared to use. Personally, I fall somewhere in between, as I like to carry more than I expect to need or want to use, but that’s mainly because I have a little extra space. Having been on the receiving end of helpful tool loan offers at the track, I try to make it possible to help those around me. This means carrying the tools needed to replace or alter parts, along with the items needed to work on the basics like wheels, brakes, and suspension.


The exact list of tools is going to change from car to car and person to person, so you won’t find a comprehensive list here. Whether pulling from your “regular” toolbox or[assembling a dedicated kit](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-essential-tools-for-a-road-trip-tool-kit/) from second-hand tools, fill your kit with items you trust but are also not sacred about. It’s common to have to modify or alter a tool during field repairs. The core of most toolkits boils down to this:


- Sockets
- Ratchet
- Wrenches
- Screwdrivers
- Sharp knife
- Various pliers
- Large and small hammer
- Impact wrench
- Torque wrench
- Jack and stands
- Work gloves
- Flashlight
- Some common-size nuts and bolts


## Fluids


Good brake fluid and some spare coolant can save someone’s day.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


These large containers of water are nice for fresh drinking and also for topping up radiators.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


While we are focused on keeping the car alive, that is only 50% of the equation. Fluids should be packed for the car and yourself in equal proportions. For the car, it’s important to have extra coolant, brake fluid, and oil, as the car might consume or require a top-up of any of those three. This is especially important if you run special or unique fluids in your car, like specific coolant or an uncommon oil weight.


It’s also important to keep fluids in you as well. Driving a street car on track is not as physical as other motorsports, but it can be surprisingly draining on your body. Fluid loss is usually worst through sweating, so just keeping up with drinking water between sessions can go a long way. A sports drink can help with electrolytes and a little sugar kick too. A good habit is taking a drink each time you take your helmet off and each time before you put it on.


## Fuel


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I’m separating this one from the other fluids because it’s that important. At least it is for me because the first time I took my Corvette to the track I had no idea what to expect for fuel consumption. It was also a track that did not have gas pumps, nor was it easy to leave and drive to a station to fill up. Instead, I brought as much as I could safely transport just in case. Even if there are fuel pumps on the track property or nearby, bringing your own fuel might be the smarter option, as it eliminates the stress of having to manage the time between on-track sessions and avoids exorbitant pricing and trouble if the pumps are non-operational or otherwise out.


## Comfort


Yes, you do end up chasing the shadow of a smaller tent, but it’s still worth it.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Tent, table, and chair take up a decent amount of space yet make the time between sessions more comfortable.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Race tracks offer varying levels of accommodation, and there often isn’t enough time between sessions to go exploring or find a chill spot to hang before getting back in the car. Bringing a chair is a given, so think past what you are sitting on and where you will be sitting. Most tracks don’t have shade trees in the middle of the paddock—usually it’s a vast expanse of pavement where the sun (or rain) beats down mercilessly.


Having a place to shelter in the shade can be as simple as bringing a pop-up canopy—should it fit in your car or tow rig. I’ve found a canopy is one of the better ways to make friends at a track day—in both directions. When I have one, people come to me to talk and hang out. When I don’t have one, I go find cool people to talk to and hang out with in their shade. A small luxury is a folding table. For years I just used the truck tailgate, or floor of my van, or the ground as my work surface, but having a table made cooking easier, and things got lost or misplaced less because everything naturally gravitated towards the table rather than cast in random directions.


## Keys


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Yeah, it’s funny to read here, but it’s really not funny to arrive at the track and go to back the car off the trailer to find a temporary paperweight. If you’re driving your car to the track, this is less of a deal for obvious reasons, but not all packing lists include a reminder to check for your keys before you leave home. Keep from forgetting items like this by making a checklist that you pack by. Yeah, I think it sounds goofy, too, but there is often enough money tied up in just getting to and enjoying a track day that I don’t want to risk having a bad time over forgetting one or two things.


***


Going to the track can be a fun and rewarding experience in so many different types of cars, but only if you can focus on the driving on track. Let this be the start of your packing list should you ever decide to try out track driving, and of course be sure to adjust it as your needs change. My track day packing has changed over the years, and yours likely will too—but we all have to start somewhere.
